paragraphs.heading: What a forecast is
paragraphs.text: Weather forecasting means using science and technology to say what the atmosphere will be like at a given place and time. Forecasters gather measurements of the present state of the air, land and ocean, then use meteorology to work out how the atmosphere will change. Forecasts were once worked out by hand, mostly from shifts in air pressure, current conditions and the look of the sky. Today they rest on computer models that weigh many factors in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Why forecasts go wrong
paragraphs.text: People still matter: someone has to choose the best model to build a forecast on, using pattern recognition and knowledge of how each model performs and where it is biased. Forecasts are imperfect because the atmosphere is chaotic, the equations need huge computing power, starting measurements carry errors, and some processes are not fully understood. So the further ahead a forecast reaches, the less accurate it becomes. Using ensembles and model consensus helps narrow the error and build confidence.

paragraphs.heading: Who uses forecasts
paragraphs.text: Weather warnings protect lives and property. Agriculture relies on temperature and rain forecasts, and so do traders in commodity markets. Power companies use temperature forecasts to estimate demand over the coming days, and many people simply check the forecast to decide what to wear. In 2009 the United States spent about $5.8 billion on forecasting, with benefits estimated at six times that.

paragraphs.heading: Old weather lore
paragraphs.text: People have tried to predict the weather informally for thousands of years. In 650 BC the Babylonians read it from cloud patterns and astrology, and around 350 BC Aristotle described weather patterns in Meteorologica. Early methods mostly relied on spotting patterns: a very red sunset, for example, was often followed by a fair day. Such sayings built up over generations into weather lore, but many have since failed rigorous statistical tests.

paragraphs.heading: The telegraph
paragraphs.text: The modern age of forecasting began with the electric telegraph in 1835. Before it, reports of distant weather moved at most around 160 km a day, and usually only 60–120 km. By the late 1840s, reports from a wide area arrived almost instantly, so forecasts could draw on conditions further upwind.

paragraphs.heading: FitzRoy names the forecast
paragraphs.text: Royal Navy officer Francis Beaufort and his protégé Robert FitzRoy are credited with turning forecasting into a science. In 1854 FitzRoy took charge of a new Board of Trade department that collected weather data at sea for sailors. After a storm in October 1859 led to the loss of the Royal Charter, he drew up charts for making predictions and called this forecasting the weather, which gave us the term. Fifteen land stations telegraphed him daily reports, his warning service for ships began in February 1861, and The Times printed the first daily forecasts that same year.
